zh.q: 五种盐溶液摆在这里，为什么非得用 pH 计一支一支量？
zh.concl: 盐溶液不一定中性：同样是「盐」，有的显酸性、有的显碱性，得先量出来才知道。
points: 四个站各回答一个不同的问题：盐的类型、温度、净水、机理。
5 支 + 对照并排、同高同光照，才看得出颜色与浑浊的差别。
pH 计是本题唯一能把「酸碱性」变成数的仪器（量程 0–14）。

zh.q: 换一种盐，pH 就变了——是盐的「出身」决定的吗？
zh.concl: 强酸强碱盐的溶液呈中性，强酸弱碱盐的溶液呈酸性，强碱弱酸盐的溶液呈碱性（教材原话）。
points: 判断酸碱性看的是「盐由哪种酸和哪种碱生成」。
NaCl、KNO₃ 的离子都不与 H⁺、OH⁻ 结合，所以呈中性。
Na₂CO₃ 的碱性比 CH₃COONa 强，因为 HCO₃⁻ 比 CH₃COOH 更难电离。

zh.q: NaCl 和 NH₄Cl 都是盐，凭什么一个中性一个酸性？
zh.concl: NH₄⁺ 与水电离出的 OH⁻ 结合生成弱电解质 NH₃·H₂O，破坏了水的电离平衡并使之右移，c(H⁺) > c(OH⁻)（教材原话）。
points: 关键不是「盐里有 H⁺」，而是「弱离子把水的 H⁺ 或 OH⁻ 抢走了」。
被抢走的是 OH⁻，水的电离平衡就往右补，于是 H⁺ 多出来。
强碱弱酸盐反过来：CO₃²⁻ 抢 H⁺，OH⁻ 多出来。

zh.q: 加水稀释，水解程度变大还是变小？
zh.concl: 加水稀释促使平衡向水解方向移动、水解程度增大；但溶液变稀，c(OH⁻) 反而减小，碱性变弱。
points: 稀释时「水解度」和「离子浓度」朝相反方向走，这是本题最容易混的一处。
判断水解程度看水解度，判断酸碱性看 c(H⁺) 或 c(OH⁻)。
所以「稀释促进水解」不能读成「稀释后碱性更强」。

zh.q: 把纯碱水加热，为什么洗油污更干净？
zh.concl: 盐类水解是吸热反应（中和反应的逆反应），加热促使平衡向水解方向移动、水解程度增大，c(OH⁻) 增大，所以热的纯碱水去油污更强。
points: 升温是「所有水解」的促进因素，不分酸式盐还是碱式盐。
油污水浴那两支试管一支加热一支不加热，就是教材的对照。
热的纯碱更「碱」，靠的是 c(OH⁻) 增大，不是温度本身。

zh.q: 较浓盐酸为什么能把 Fe³⁺ 的水解压下去？
zh.concl: 增大 c(H⁺) 使水解平衡向逆方向移动、抑制 Fe³⁺ 水解；所以实验室配制 FeCl₃ 溶液要先把晶体溶于较浓盐酸再稀释。
points: 加酸的结果要分盐：酸式盐被抑制，碱式盐被促进。
CH₃COONa 那一支看的是「CH₃COO⁻ 转化的比例」——H⁺ 是被直接加进去、把 OH⁻ 与 CH₃COO⁻ 消耗掉，不是同一个可逆水解自己变大。
抑制 Fe³⁺ 水解的代价是溶液更酸，所以配溶液只能先加酸再稀释。

zh.q: 两勺泥水加点铁盐、铝盐，凭什么能变清？
zh.concl: 可溶性的铝盐、铁盐靠水解生成的胶体吸附悬浮颗粒而净水，不是杀菌消毒。
points: 起作用的是「水解生成的胶体」，不是离子本身。
三支试管必有一支不加净水剂作对照，否则看不出澄清是净水剂带来的。
明矾 KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O 与 FeCl₃ 是同一原理，教材练习第 1 题就考它。

zh.q: 煮沸 FeCl₃ 溶液会变红褐色，可蒸干它为什么又得不到 FeCl₃？
zh.concl: 加热使水解趋于完全，HCl 又随蒸气挥发，平衡一直向右移；所以蒸干、灼烧得不到 FeCl₃。
points: 这是本课的错误操作示范：想用蒸干的办法拿到 FeCl₃，实际拿到的是 Fe(OH)₃ 再分解成 Fe₂O₃。
错在哪一步：HCl 是水解产物，一挥发就不再是可逆平衡，水解被「抽干」。
胶体是红褐色透明的（丁达尔效应可验证），与泥水那种浑浊不是一回事。

zh.q: 考核：按教材的做法配一份 0.010 mol/L 的 FeCl₃ 溶液
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：把「先溶于较浓盐酸、再稀释、不加热」三件事同时照顾好，水解度才压得住。
points: 加酸是主手段：0.070 mol/L 的盐酸把水解度从 54 % 压到 8.2 %。
温度是敌人：一加热就回到 49 %，比加酸的效果还快。
浓度按教材 0.010 mol/L，不能靠稀释蒙过去。

en.q: Five salt solutions are set out here. Why must we measure them one by one with a pH meter?
en.concl: Salt solutions are not necessarily neutral: some "salts" are acidic and some basic, and you only know after measuring.
points: Each of the four stations answers a different question: type of salt, temperature, water purification, mechanism.
Only with 5 tubes + a control side by side, at the same height and lighting, can differences in color and cloudiness be seen.
The pH meter is the only instrument here that turns "acidity" into a number (range 0–14).

en.q: Change the salt and the pH changes. Is it decided by the salt's "parentage"?
en.concl: Solutions of salts of a strong acid and strong base are neutral, of a strong acid and weak base acidic, and of a strong base and weak acid basic (textbook wording).
points: To judge acidity, look at "which acid and which base the salt comes from".
The ions of NaCl and KNO₃ do not combine with H⁺ or OH⁻, so they are neutral.
Na₂CO₃ is more basic than CH₃COONa because HCO₃⁻ ionizes even less than CH₃COOH.

en.q: NaCl and NH₄Cl are both salts. Why is one neutral and the other acidic?
en.concl: NH₄⁺ combines with OH⁻ from water's ionization to form the weak electrolyte NH₃·H₂O, upsetting water's ionization equilibrium and shifting it right, so c(H⁺) > c(OH⁻) (textbook wording).
points: The key is not "the salt contains H⁺", but "the weak ion takes H⁺ or OH⁻ from water".
When OH⁻ is taken, water's ionization equilibrium shifts right to make up, so H⁺ ends up in excess.
Salts of a strong base and weak acid work the other way: CO₃²⁻ takes H⁺, leaving excess OH⁻.

en.q: Does diluting with water increase or decrease the extent of hydrolysis?
en.concl: Diluting with water shifts the equilibrium toward hydrolysis and increases its extent; but the solution is more dilute, so c(OH⁻) actually falls and it is less basic.
points: On dilution the "degree of hydrolysis" and the "ion concentration" move in opposite directions, the easiest point to confuse in this topic.
Judge the extent of hydrolysis by the degree of hydrolysis, and acidity by c(H⁺) or c(OH⁻).
So "dilution promotes hydrolysis" must not be read as "more basic after dilution".

en.q: Why does hot soda water remove grease better?
en.concl: Salt hydrolysis is endothermic (the reverse of neutralization); heating shifts the equilibrium toward hydrolysis and increases its extent, so c(OH⁻) rises and hot soda water removes grease better.
points: Heating promotes "all hydrolysis", whether the salt gives an acidic or a basic solution.
Of the two greasy tubes in the water bath, one heated and one not: that is the textbook's control.
Hot soda is "more basic" because c(OH⁻) rises, not because of the temperature itself.

en.q: Why can fairly concentrated hydrochloric acid hold back the hydrolysis of Fe³⁺?
en.concl: Raising c(H⁺) shifts the hydrolysis equilibrium backward and suppresses Fe³⁺ hydrolysis; so in the lab FeCl₃ crystals are first dissolved in fairly concentrated hydrochloric acid and then diluted.
points: The effect of adding acid depends on the salt: acidic salts are suppressed, basic salts promoted.
For CH₃COONa we look at "the fraction of CH₃COO⁻ converted": H⁺ added directly consumes OH⁻ and CH₃COO⁻, rather than the reversible hydrolysis itself growing.
The price of suppressing Fe³⁺ hydrolysis is a more acidic solution, so the solution can only be prepared by adding acid first, then diluting.

en.q: Two spoonfuls of muddy water with a bit of iron or aluminum salt: how can it turn clear?
en.concl: Soluble aluminum and iron salts purify water because the colloids formed by hydrolysis adsorb suspended particles; they do not kill germs.
points: What works is "the colloid formed by hydrolysis", not the ions themselves.
One of the three tubes must have no coagulant as a control, or you cannot tell the clearing comes from the coagulant.
Alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O works on the same principle as FeCl₃; textbook exercise 1 tests exactly this.

en.q: Boiling FeCl₃ solution turns it red-brown. Why can't you get FeCl₃ back by evaporating it to dryness?
en.concl: Heating drives hydrolysis toward completion while HCl escapes with the vapor, so the equilibrium keeps shifting right; evaporating and heating strongly cannot give FeCl₃.
points: This is the lesson's demonstration of a wrong procedure: trying to get FeCl₃ by evaporating to dryness actually gives Fe(OH)₃, which then decomposes to Fe₂O₃.
Where it goes wrong: HCl is a hydrolysis product, and once it escapes the equilibrium is no longer reversible, so hydrolysis is "drained dry".
The colloid is red-brown and transparent (check with the Tyndall effect), not the same as cloudy muddy water.

en.q: Check: prepare a 0.010 mol/L FeCl₃ solution the way the textbook does
en.concl: The check has no new conclusion: only by handling "dissolve in fairly concentrated hydrochloric acid first, then dilute, no heating" at once can hydrolysis be held down.
points: Adding acid is the main tool: 0.070 mol/L hydrochloric acid brings hydrolysis from 54 % down to 8.2 %.
Temperature is the enemy: as soon as it is heated, hydrolysis is back to 49 %, faster than the acid can act.
The concentration follows the textbook's 0.010 mol/L; you cannot get by through dilution.
